extracted.intended_audience: screenwriters, fiction writers, and students of story structure
extracted.subtask_short: scene and subplot design for screenplays
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on designing subplots and scenes for screenplays: how subplots should relate to a central plot and Controlling Idea, and how individual scenes must function as Turning Points with setups/payoffs and dynamic emotional transitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: An idea holds the film together
rubrics_metrics.description: What then holds the film together? An idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by PARENTHOOD and DINER: films 'play variations on the notion' that parenthood can't be won or that men can't communicate with women. The central unifying idea (Controlling Idea) should be the glue that gives coherence to varied scenes and subplots.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a setup subplot when the Central Plot's Inciting Incident must be delayed
rubrics_metrics.description: When the Central Plot’s Inciting Incident must be delayed, a setup subplot may be needed to open the storytelling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ROCKY, CHINATOWN, CASABLANCA used subplots to fill early story vacuum and acquaint the audience with protagonist and world so they'll react fully to the eventual Inciting Incident. A setup subplot dramatizes the Central Plot’s exposition indirectly and fluidly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use subplots to complicate the Central Plot (source of antagonism)
rubrics_metrics.description: A subplot may be used to complicate the Central Plot — as an additional source of antagonism for the protagonist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Love Story inside Crime Stories (SEA OF LOVE, BLACK WIDOW, THE VERDICT). Subplots add dimension, comic/romantic relief, but primarily should make life harder for the protagonist. Their chief purpose is to create obstacles, not merely diversion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control balance of emphasis between Central Plot and subplot
rubrics_metrics.description: The balance of emphasis between the Central Plot and subplot has to be carefully controlled, or the writer risks losing focus on the primary story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dangers: a setup subplot can mislead audience about genre (e.g., ROCKY's opening love story required careful handling). If subplot protagonists differ, avoid drawing too much empathy to them. To deemphasize a subplot, keep some of its elements (Inciting Incident, climaxes, Crisis, Climax, Resolution) offscreen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Turn a subplot into the Central Plot if it demands greater focus
rubrics_metrics.description: If, as you develop your screenplay, your subplot seems to demand greater focus and empathy, then reconsider the overall design and turn your subplot into the Central Plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design must be flexible; allow story to be reorganized so that the primary emotional focus remains intact rather than forcing an ill-fitting subordinate line.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subplot must resonate thematically or causally with the Central Plot
rubrics_metrics.description: If a subplot doesn’t thematically contradict or resonate the Controlling Idea of the main plot, if it doesn’t set up the introduction of the main plot’s Inciting Incident, or complicate the action on the main plot, if it merely runs alongside, it will split the story and destroy its effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Audience expects aesthetic unity: every element must relate structurally or thematically. If the audience can’t find the relationship, it will disengage and attempt to force unity, often failing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make interior life visual in screen adaptations
rubrics_metrics.description: The screenwriter must reinvent a novel’s interior life: 'The screenwriting is the art of making the mental physical.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on dialogue or narration to describe inner thought. Create visual correlatives (images of character choice and action) to express inner conflict; use techniques like film-within-film (KISS OF THE SPIDER WOMAN) to visualize fantasy or inner planes.

rubrics_metrics.name: A scene is a story in miniature unified around desire, action, conflict, and change
rubrics_metrics.description: A scene is an action through conflict in a unity or continuity of time and space that turns the value-charged condition of a character's life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No matter location or length, a scene must be unified around a Scene-Objective (an aspect of the character's Super-Objective/Spine). Avoid writing scenes that are flat exposition; aim for desire, choice under pressure, and an unforeseen reaction that changes outer fortunes or inner life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Every scene should function as a Turning Point (minor/moderate/major)
rubrics_metrics.description: A scene causes change in a minor, albeit significant way. A Sequence Climax causes a moderate reversal; an Act Climax causes a major reversal. Strive for every scene to be a minor, moderate, or major Turning Point rather than static display.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Turning Points are measured by the magnitude of reversal they create. Plan scenes so they produce movement (value change) in the story’s trajectory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effects of Turning Points: surprise, increased curiosity, insight, and new direction
rubrics_metrics.description: The effects of Turning Points are fourfold: surprise, increased curiosity, insight, and new direction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: TRADING PLACES and WALL STREET produce 'why?' questions that send the audience back through prior scenes to find answers. Well-layered setups provide those answers and produce a rush of insight which propels curiosity and new story directions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Turning Points provoke the audience to seek answers in prior material
rubrics_metrics.description: When a gap opens between expectation and result, it jolts the audience with surprise; the audience then rushes back through the story seeking answers, and in a well-designed work these answers have been quietly but carefully layered in.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design set-ups so the audience's retrospective search yields satisfying insight; future Turning Points must build on these discoveries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Setups and Payoffs: plant knowledge to be delivered later
rubrics_metrics.description: To express our vision scene by scene we crack open the surface of our fictional reality and send the audience back to gain insight. These insights must be shaped into Setups and Payoffs: to set up means to layer in knowledge; to pay off means to close the gap by delivering that knowledge to the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: CHINATOWN, THE EMPIRE STRIKES BACK, SULLIVAN’S TRAVELS. Setups should have one meaning initially and, upon payoff, take on a deeper meaning (sometimes multiple levels). Payoffs often become setups for further payoffs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plant setups with calibrated subtlety—rememberable but not obvious
rubrics_metrics.description: Setups must be planted firmly enough so that when the audience's mind hurls back, they're remembered. If setups are too subtle, the audience will miss the point. If too heavy-handed, the Turning Point will be anticipated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure modes: overprepare the obvious (predictability) or underprepare the unusual (audience miss). Adjust the firmness of setup to the target audience's story literacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjust setup prominence to target audience sophistication
rubrics_metrics.description: The firmness of the setup must be adjusted to the target audience. We set up more prominently for youth audiences because they're less story literate; auteurs like Bergman use subtle setups intended for well-educated, experienced audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider audience's ability to perceive layered meanings when deciding how overt to make your setups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Setups can have multiple levels of meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: It's possible that a single setup may have meanings hidden to a third or fourth level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example CHINATOWN: Noah Cross's early line 'My daughter' has initial and deeper meanings revealed later. Use multi-level setups to reward retrospective insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Payoffs often set up future payoffs—use juggling of setups/payoffs to propel story
rubrics_metrics.description: Once the setup closes the gap, that payoff will probably become another setup for payoffs ahead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'juggling act' of setting up and paying off repeatedly is a source of creative structural momentum—each payoff should seed the next set of audience questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-expression occurs primarily through Turning Points, not decorative language
rubrics_metrics.description: Our most powerful means of self-expression is the unique way we turn the story. Language is a tool and must never become a decorative end of its own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid substituting information for insight (explaining meanings via dialogue or voice-over). Even exquisite prose cannot replace the global insight produced by well-placed setups and Turning Points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use imagination first; logic can be made retroactive
rubrics_metrics.description: Imagination—the willingness to think any crazy idea—is primary. Logic is retroactive: you can go back and layer in reasons to make an initially illogical but revealing idea make sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encouragement to entertain unlikely, provocative ideas (most will be useless) because one may reveal a structural key; then rewrite earlier scenes to plant motivations and make the idea logical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional Transitions: emotion is produced by value transitions under empathy conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: We do not move the emotions of an audience by showing tears or calling for music; rather, we render the precise experience necessary to cause an emotion and take the audience through that experience. Turning Points deliver insight and create the dynamics of emotion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three necessary conditions for emotion: (1) empathize with character, (2) know what the character wants and want them to have it, (3) understand the values at stake. Then a change in values moves emotions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of Diminishing Returns for emotion — vary emotional charges
rubrics_metrics.description: The Law of Diminishing Returns: the more often we experience something, the less effect it has. Emotional experience cannot be repeated back-to-back with effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you place similar emotional scenes consecutively, each subsequent one has reduced impact and can even reverse effect (audience laughs at repeated tragedy). Alternate positive/negative transitions or escalate contrasts; exceptions exist when contrasts are great enough (e.g., argument then murder makes the argument seem positive retrospectively).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish feeling (mood) from emotion; use mood as foreshadowing
rubrics_metrics.description: Once a transition creates an emotion, feeling (a long-term background state) colors which specific emotion we experience. In film, feeling is mood, created by textural elements (lighting, tempo, casting, production design, score).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use mood to make emotions specific and as a form of foreshadowing; mood plus dynamic scene transitions produce targeted audience feelings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scene-Objective must relate to Super-Objective/Spine and force choice under pressure
rubrics_metrics.description: In each scene a character pursues a desire related to his immediate time and place. This Scene-Objective must be an aspect of his Super-Objective or Spine. Within the scene the character acts by choosing under pressure between actions, and unexpected reactions create the gap that becomes the Turning Point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design scenes so the immediate objective advances the larger story goal; ensure choices are pressured and produce unforeseen consequences that alter values and move the story forward.
